module_title: Layer Housing and Laying Nest Management

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Housing System for Your Layer Flock
lessons.body: Selecting a housing system is one of the most consequential decisions you will make as a layer farmer in Africa. It affects your capital outlay, labour requirements, disease pressure, egg quality, and ultimately your profit margin. There is no single best system for the entire continent because conditions vary from the humid coastal zones of West Africa to the highlands of East Africa and the semi-arid regions of Southern Africa. Your choice must respond to your climate, your market, your budget, and your management capacity. The three broad categories are deep litter, cage or battery systems, and free-range or semi-intensive systems. Each has a place, and each demands a different level of investment and skill. Deep litter is the most common starting point for small and medium-scale producers. Birds are kept on a floor covered with bedding material such as wood shavings, rice husks, maize cobs, or chopped straw. The litter absorbs moisture, buffers temperature, and allows birds to express natural scratching behaviour. In hot African climates, deep litter is cooler than cages and reduces heat stress, which directly protects egg production. However, litter must be managed carefully. Wet litter produces ammonia, which damages the respiratory tract and causes eye problems. You must top up litter regularly, remove caked patches, and ensure the house has adequate ventilation. A good rule is to provide 6 to 8 birds per square metre in open-sided tropical housing, though this can rise to 10 in well-ventilated highland areas. Cage systems offer the highest stocking density and the best control over disease and egg hygiene. Eggs roll out of reach of the birds, so they stay clean and are less likely to be broken or eaten. Feed conversion is better because birds expend less energy moving. In Africa, cages are increasingly used by commercial producers near cities where land is expensive and theft is a concern. The main criticisms are welfare-related and the high initial cost of galvanised wire and structural steel. If you choose cages, invest in quality materials because cheap wire rusts quickly in humid conditions and injures birds. Free-range and semi-intensive systems appeal to the growing market for organic or village eggs, which often fetch premium prices in urban supermarkets and hotels. Birds forage for insects, seeds, and green matter, reducing feed costs. But production is lower, predation is a constant threat, and egg collection is labour-intensive. In many African contexts, a hybrid approach works best: a solid house with a fenced run, supplemented with balanced feed. When planning your house, prioritise orientation. In the northern hemisphere tropics, face the long axis east to west to reduce direct sun on the side walls. In the southern hemisphere, the same principle applies. Open sides should allow cross-ventilation but be fitted with wire mesh to keep out wild birds, rodents, and snakes. Roof overhang of at least one metre protects against driving rain. The floor should be raised 30 to 45 centimetres above ground level and made of concrete or packed earth with a damp-proof course. This prevents dampness and makes cleaning easier. Water supply must be reliable. A layer drinks 200 to 300 millilitres per day depending on temperature. In hot weather, this can double. Install nipple drinkers or bell drinkers that are easy to clean and do not spill. Place them so that birds cannot roost on top and contaminate the water. Feeders should be designed to prevent billing out and should be raised to the level of the birds backs as they grow. Lighting is another critical factor. Laying hens need 14 to 16 hours of light per day to sustain production. In equatorial regions, natural day length is fairly constant at around 12 hours, so you may need supplemental lighting in the evening or early morning. Use energy-efficient LED bulbs and a simple timer. In areas with unreliable electricity, consider solar-powered lighting systems, which are now affordable and widely available. Finally, think about expansion. A house that is too small forces you to crowd birds, which increases stress, disease, and cannibalism. Build with future growth in mind. If you plan to keep 500 layers, design the structure so you can add a second or third block without rebuilding the entire system. Record every cost, from nails to roofing sheets, so you know your true depreciation and can price your eggs profitably. Housing is not a one-time expense; it is an asset that determines your farms productivity for years. Choose wisely, build durably, and adapt to your local climate and market.

lessons.title: Designing and Equipping the Laying House
lessons.body: Once you have chosen your housing system, the next step is to design and equip the laying house for maximum efficiency and bird comfort. A well-designed house reduces labour, prevents disease, and keeps eggs clean. In Africa, where many farms operate with limited electricity and water, design must be practical and low-maintenance. Start with the site. Choose a well-drained area that is slightly elevated to avoid flooding during the rainy season. Avoid low-lying areas where water collects, because dampness leads to respiratory disease and foot problems. The site should be at least 30 metres away from other poultry houses to reduce cross-contamination. If you keep different age groups, separate them by distance or solid barriers. The house should be accessible for feed delivery and egg collection, even during wet weather. A good access road or path saves time and prevents eggs from being shaken and cracked during transport. The floor is the foundation of a healthy house. Concrete is best because it is easy to wash, disinfect, and rat-proof. If concrete is too expensive, use compacted murram or laterite covered with a plastic vapour barrier and then a layer of sand. The floor should slope gently towards a drain or the door so that water from cleaning runs out. Never allow water to pool inside the house. For deep litter, apply 5 to 8 centimetres of dry bedding. In humid areas, use rice husks or wood shavings because they resist mould better than straw. Stir the litter weekly and remove wet patches immediately. Walls should be open-sided with wire mesh of 25 to 50 millimetres aperture. This keeps out wild birds, which can carry avian influenza, and prevents rodents from entering. In hot climates, the open sides allow cooling breezes. In cooler highland areas, you may need to cover part of the sides with curtains or polythene sheets that can be rolled up during the day. The roof should be insulated or made of reflective material to reduce heat radiation. In many parts of Africa, corrugated iron sheets are common, but they absorb heat and make the house unbearable at midday. Paint the roof white or use aluminium foil insulation under the sheets. A thatched roof is cooler but requires maintenance and can harbour insects. A double roof with an air gap is an excellent compromise. Inside the house, provide perches or roosts for birds to sleep on. This is especially important in deep litter systems. Perches should be 5 to 8 centimetres wide, made of smooth timber, and placed 60 to 90 centimetres above the floor. Allow 15 to 20 centimetres of perch space per bird. Perches reduce contact with litter, lowering the risk of breast blisters and parasitic infections. They also make birds easier to catch at night if you need to inspect them. Nest boxes are the heart of egg production. A good nest box is dark, private, and lined with clean bedding. Hens prefer to lay in a quiet, enclosed space. Provide one nest box for every five hens. If you have 500 hens, that means 100 nest boxes. They can be arranged in tiers to save space. Each box should be about 30 centimetres wide, 35 centimetres deep, and 35 centimetres high. Place them at least 60 centimetres above the floor to discourage birds from sleeping in them. A lip at the entrance prevents eggs from rolling out. Collect eggs at least twice a day, preferably three times in hot weather, to prevent breakage and reduce the chance of hens eating eggs. Feeders and drinkers must be designed for hygiene and efficiency. Trough feeders with a lip that prevents billing out are good, but they must be cleaned daily. Tube feeders are better because they hold more feed and reduce labour. Hang them from the ceiling so they can be adjusted as birds grow. Allow 10 centimetres of feeding space per bird. For drinkers, nipple systems are the gold standard because they keep water clean and reduce spillage. If you use bell drinkers, place them on a wire platform so birds cannot stand in them and foul the water. Provide 2.5 centimetres of drinking space per bird. Water must be available at all times. In hot weather, a layer can drink up to 500 millilitres per day. If water runs out for even a few hours, egg production drops and shells become thin. Install a storage tank and a simple gravity-fed system if piped water is unreliable. Lighting should be uniform throughout the house. Use LED bulbs of 5 to 10 watts, spaced evenly, and clean them regularly because dust reduces light output. A timer ensures consistent day length. In off-grid areas, solar panels with battery storage are a worthwhile investment. Finally, keep records of everything: feed consumed, eggs collected, mortality, and medication. These records tell you which parts of your house design are working and which need improvement. A well-equipped house pays for itself through higher egg production, lower mortality, and less labour.

lessons.title: Managing Laying Nests for Clean, Saleable Eggs
lessons.body: Egg quality is the difference between a profitable layer farm and one that struggles to sell its produce. In many African markets, buyers judge eggs by shell cleanliness, size, and uniformity. A dirty egg is discounted or rejected, even if it is perfectly safe to eat. The laying nest is where egg quality begins. If nests are poorly designed or managed, you will get cracked, dirty, and broken eggs, and you will lose money. This lesson focuses on practical nest management for clean, saleable eggs. First, understand hen behaviour. A hen seeks a quiet, dark, and comfortable place to lay. If she cannot find a suitable nest, she will lay on the floor. Floor eggs are almost always dirty, cracked, or eaten. Once a hen develops the habit of laying on the floor, it is difficult to break. Therefore, you must provide attractive nests from the moment the pullets come into lay, usually at 18 to 20 weeks of age. Introduce the nests before the first egg appears. Place a few dummy eggs or golf balls in the nests to show the hens where to lay. Some farmers also leave a few eggs in the nests for the first few days, but be careful not to leave them too long because they can rot and spread bacteria. Nest design matters. The ideal nest is a dark box with a slatted or wire floor covered with clean, dry bedding. The bedding should be soft but not too deep, because deep bedding can bury eggs and make them hard to find. Wood shavings, rice husks, or chopped straw work well. Avoid sawdust from treated timber, which can be toxic. The nest should have a lip at the front to keep eggs from rolling out and a roof to keep birds from roosting on top. If birds roost on the nest, they will contaminate it with droppings. A sloped roof or a wire mesh top prevents this. Nest boxes can be individual or communal. Individual boxes are easier to manage because you can inspect each one and replace soiled bedding quickly. Communal nests, also called roll-away nests, are popular in commercial farms because they allow eggs to roll onto a collection tray, keeping them clean and reducing labour. However, roll-away nests are more expensive and require careful installation to ensure eggs roll smoothly without cracking. For most small and medium farms in Africa, individual wooden or plastic nest boxes are the best choice. Place nests in the quietest part of the house, away from doors and feeders. Hens prefer a dimly lit area. If the house is very bright, hang a curtain or sack in front of the nests to create shade. The nests should be raised 60 to 90 centimetres above the floor. This height discourages birds from sleeping in them and makes egg collection easier for you. Provide one nest for every five hens. If you have too few nests, hens will queue, and some will lay on the floor. If you have too many, you waste space and bedding. Bedding management is a daily task. Remove soiled bedding every morning and replace it with clean, dry material. Eggs laid on dirty bedding pick up bacteria that can cause food poisoning in consumers. In hot, humid climates, damp bedding grows mould, which causes respiratory problems in hens and contaminates eggs. Keep a supply of dry bedding near the house so you can replace it immediately. Never use bedding that has been treated with pesticides or fungicides. Collect eggs at least twice a day, and three times in hot weather. In temperatures above 30 degrees Celsius, an egg can lose quality within hours. Collect in the morning and late afternoon, and again at midday if possible. Use clean, dry hands or a soft basket. Never use a wire bucket because it can crack shells. After collection, move eggs to a cool, shaded room. Do not wash eggs unless you have a specific market that demands it. Washing removes the natural protective bloom on the shell, allowing bacteria to enter. If eggs are dirty, wipe them with a dry cloth or fine sandpaper. Only wash eggs if you can do it with warm water and a sanitizer, and then refrigerate them immediately. In most African markets, unwashed eggs stored in a cool room sell well. Train your workers to handle eggs gently. Cracked eggs are a direct loss. Store eggs in clean trays, pointed end down, in a cool, dark place. Do not stack trays too high, because the weight can crack the bottom eggs. If you have a refrigerator, store eggs at 10 to 15 degrees Celsius. Without refrigeration, keep them in the coolest part of the house, away from sunlight and strong odours. Eggs absorb smells, so never store them near onions, paraffin, or chemicals. Finally, keep records of egg production per house, per day. If you see a sudden drop in production or an increase in dirty eggs, investigate immediately. It could be a nest management problem, a disease, or a feed issue. Clean nests and careful handling are simple, low-cost practices that directly increase your income. Make them a non-negotiable part of your daily routine.

lessons.title: Litter, Ventilation, and Disease Control in Layer Houses
lessons.body: The environment inside your layer house determines whether your birds stay healthy and productive or succumb to disease and stress. Litter management, ventilation, and biosecurity are three pillars of environmental control. In Africa, where many farms are open-sided and rely on natural ventilation, these practices require daily attention. This lesson gives you practical steps to keep your house dry, well-ventilated, and free of disease. Litter is the bedding material on the floor of deep litter houses. Its purpose is to absorb moisture, cushion birds, and allow natural scratching. Good litter is dry, loose, and crumbly. Wet litter is a sign of poor ventilation, leaking drinkers, or overcrowding. When litter is wet, bacteria break down uric acid in droppings and release ammonia. Ammonia has a sharp smell and irritates the eyes and respiratory tract. If you can smell ammonia at bird level, the concentration is already too high. High ammonia reduces feed intake, lowers egg production, and predisposes birds to respiratory infections. To manage litter, start with a good depth: 5 to 8 centimetres in hot climates, up to 10 centimetres in cooler areas. Use materials that are absorbent and free of mould. Rice husks are excellent in humid zones. Wood shavings are good but must be from untreated timber. Maize cobs are cheap but must be ground or chopped. Straw is less absorbent and can become mouldy quickly. Stir the litter at least twice a week to turn the top layer and release trapped moisture. Remove caked or wet patches immediately. If the whole house is wet, find the source. Check drinkers for leaks, repair the roof, and improve drainage around the house. In very humid areas, you may need to add fresh litter more often. Ventilation is the movement of air through the house. It removes heat, moisture, ammonia, and dust, and brings in fresh oxygen. In open-sided houses, ventilation depends on wind and the stack effect, where warm air rises and escapes through the roof. To maximise natural ventilation, orient the house so the long axis faces the prevailing wind. Keep the sides open and free of obstructions such as feed bags or vegetation. If you use curtains, roll them up during the day and lower them only during heavy rain or cold nights. The roof should have a ridge vent or open ridge to let hot air escape. In closed houses, you need mechanical ventilation using fans. This is expensive and requires reliable electricity, so it is rare in most African layer farms. If you use fans, install them on the opposite side from the air inlets and ensure they are cleaned regularly. Poor ventilation causes heat stress, which is a major killer of layers in hot climates. A hen suffering from heat stress pants, holds her wings away from her body, and reduces feed intake. Egg production drops, and shells become thin. To reduce heat stress, provide shade, increase airflow, and ensure cool water is always available. You can also wet the roof or use sprinklers on the roof to cool the house. Biosecurity is the set of practices that prevent disease from entering your farm. It is not optional. One outbreak of Newcastle disease or avian influenza can wipe out your flock and your investment. Start with a footbath at the entrance to each house. Use a disinfectant that is effective against viruses, and change the solution daily. Keep a pair of boots and a coat for each house. Do not move between houses without changing boots and washing hands. Limit visitors. If you must allow visitors, make them wear protective clothing and walk through the footbath. Keep wild birds out. They carry avian influenza and Newcastle disease. Use wire mesh on all openings and repair any holes immediately. Control rodents and insects. Rats eat feed, spread disease, and stress birds. Keep feed in sealed containers and clear vegetation around the house. Flies breed in wet litter and manure. Keep the area dry and use fly traps or approved insecticides. Vaccinate your flock according to a schedule recommended by your local veterinary authority. Common vaccines include Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis, fowl pox, and Mareks disease. Store vaccines correctly and use clean syringes. Never reuse needles. Isolate sick birds immediately. If you see birds with respiratory distress, diarrhoea, or a drop in egg production, call a vet. Do not wait. Early action saves the flock. Finally, keep records of mortality, medication, and vaccinations. These records help you identify patterns and prevent future problems. A healthy house is a profitable house. Invest time in litter, ventilation, and biosecurity every single day.

lessons.title: Labour, Records, and Economics of Layer Housing
lessons.body: A layer farm is a business, and like any business, it must be managed with numbers. Housing and nest management are not just technical matters; they have direct economic consequences. Poor housing increases mortality, reduces egg production, and raises labour costs. Good housing, on the other hand, pays for itself through higher output and lower losses. This lesson covers labour planning, record keeping, and the economics of layer housing in an African context. Labour is often the largest recurring cost after feed. In small farms, family labour is common. In larger farms, you need hired workers. The number of workers depends on your system. Deep litter houses require more labour for litter management, egg collection, and cleaning. Cage systems require less labour for cleaning but more for inspecting birds and maintaining equipment. As a rule, one worker can manage 1,000 to 1,500 layers in a well-designed deep litter house, or 2,000 to 3,000 in a cage system. But these numbers assume good housing, reliable water, and mechanised feed delivery. If you carry feed by hand and water by bucket, you need more workers. Train your workers well. A trained worker collects eggs gently, spots sick birds early, and keeps records accurately. Untrained workers break eggs, miss sick birds, and forget to close doors. Invest in training. Teach workers how to handle birds, how to clean drinkers, how to identify common diseases, and how to record data. Pay them fairly and on time. A motivated worker is your best asset. Provide clear written instructions for daily, weekly, and monthly tasks. Use a simple checklist that workers tick off. This reduces mistakes and makes supervision easier. Record keeping is the backbone of profitable farming. You cannot manage what you do not measure. Keep records of feed consumption, egg production, mortality, medication, and sales. For housing, record the cost of construction, repairs, and depreciation. Depreciation is the loss in value of your house and equipment over time. If you build a house for 10,000 dollars and it lasts 10 years, the annual depreciation is 1,000 dollars. You must include this in your cost of production. Otherwise, you will think you are making a profit when you are actually losing money. Egg production records should be daily. Count eggs per house, per day. Calculate the laying percentage by dividing the number of eggs by the number of hens and multiplying by 100. A good flock peaks at 90 to 95 percent and then declines slowly. If your laying percentage drops suddenly, investigate. It could be a disease, a feed problem, or a housing issue such as poor ventilation or dirty nests. Feed records tell you the feed conversion ratio, which is the kilograms of feed needed to produce one kilogram of eggs. A good ratio is around 2.0 to 2.2 kilograms of feed per kilogram of eggs. If your ratio is higher, your feed is being wasted or your birds are stressed. Mortality records help you identify disease outbreaks and culling needs. A mortality rate of 0.5 percent per month is acceptable. Higher rates mean something is wrong. Use a simple notebook or a spreadsheet. If you have a smartphone, use a free app for record keeping. The key is consistency. Record every day, even if the numbers are small. Economics of housing: Before you build, calculate the return on investment. A layer house is a long-term asset. If you spend 5,000 dollars on a house for 1,000 birds, and each bird produces 300 eggs per year, you get 300,000 eggs. If you sell at 0.10 dollars per egg, that is 30,000 dollars in revenue. Even after feed, labour, and other costs, the house pays for itself in a few years. But if you build a cheap house that leaks, floods, and causes disease, you will lose birds and money. Quality housing is cheaper in the long run. Consider the cost of egg breakage. If 5 percent of your eggs are dirty or cracked, you lose 5 percent of your revenue. Better nests and careful handling can reduce this to 1 percent. That is a direct increase in profit. Consider the cost of mortality. If 10 percent of your birds die from preventable diseases, you lose 10 percent of your potential production. Good ventilation and biosecurity can keep mortality below 5 percent. Finally, think about your market. If you sell to supermarkets or hotels, they may require clean, uniform eggs. That means you need roll-away nests or very careful nest management. If you sell to local consumers, they may accept slightly dirty eggs at a lower price. Know your market and design your housing and nests to meet its standards. In summary, treat your layer house as a factory. The birds are the machines, the feed is the raw material, and the eggs are the product. Your job is to keep the factory running efficiently. Plan labour, keep records, and calculate your costs. That is how you turn a small flock into a profitable business.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Layer House Measurements, Stocking Rates, and Cost Benchmarks for African Farms

This Practical Reference lesson converts the design theory from Module 5 into numbers you can apply on a farm today. It covers the three decisions that most often determine whether a layer enterprise in Africa makes money: how many birds you put in a given space, how you build the shell of the house at the lowest cost that still protects the flock, and what the house itself costs per bird over its working life. Every figure below is drawn from published extension and research sources, with the source named so you can verify and adapt it to your own climate, breed, and market.

The guiding business principle is simple: the house is a fixed cost that must be spread over as many saleable eggs as possible. Overstock and you lose birds to heat stress, disease, and feather pecking. Understock and your cost per egg rises because the same roof, walls, and labour are carrying fewer birds. The target is the highest stocking density at which mortality, feed conversion, and egg quality remain stable through the whole laying cycle.

Sources: Aviagen, Bovans Management Handbook (space allowance tables); FAO, Poultry Development Review (2013); and university extension guidance from the University of Georgia Cooperative Extension, Layer Housing and Space Requirements. Figures assume moderate tropical temperatures (18â28 Â°C). In areas where daytime temperatures regularly exceed 30 Â°C, add 10â20 % more floor and feeder space to reduce heat stress and competitive feeding.

Sources: Figures compiled and adapted from ILRI, Smallholder Poultry Production and Marketing (ILRI, 2019); FAO, Poultry Sector Development country reports; and the University of Georgia Cooperative Extension poultry enterprise budgets. Costs vary widely by country, exchange rate, and timber or steel prices. Use these as a starting benchmark and replace with your own local quotes before committing capital. The last row is calculated by dividing total house cost by the total number of eggs expected over the laying cycle, and is the single most useful figure for comparing housing options.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HEALTH, CHEMICALS, AND FOOD SAFETY

Litter, dust, and ammonia in layer houses are occupational and food-safety hazards. Follow these rules without exception:

  • Never enter a house with ammonia strong enough to sting your eyes or nose. Ammonia above 25 ppm damages birds' respiratory tracts and reduces egg production. Ventilate first, then enter.
  • Wear a dust mask and gloves when cleaning out litter, handling manure, or applying any disinfectant or insecticide. Poultry dust can carry bacteria and fungal spores harmful to humans.
  • Store all chemicals â disinfectants, insecticides, rodenticides, vaccines â in a locked cabinet away from feed and eggs, in original labelled containers. Never decant into drink bottles.
  • Observe the withdrawal period on every product used on or near laying birds. Eggs from treated birds may be unsafe for sale or consumption during withdrawal.
  • Wash hands with soap after handling birds, litter, or eggs, and before eating. Keep eggs out of contact with manure, dirty litter, and broken shells.
  • Dispose of dead birds immediately by deep burial or incineration. Never sell or consume dead birds. Report sudden multiple deaths to your veterinary officer.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Calculate floor area first: length Ã width in metres Ã 10,000 = cmÂ². Divide by your target cmÂ²/bird (1,100â1,500 for deep litter) to get maximum bird number. Write this number on the house wall.
  • Check feeder and drinker space against Table 1 before you buy equipment. Under-supplied feeders cause pecking and uneven flock weight.
  • Confirm eave height is at least 2.4 m and the ridge is open. Hot air must escape above the birds, not sit on their backs.
  • Allow 10â20 % extra space in hot regions or during the peak of the dry season.
  • Provide one nest per 5â6 hens, raised 45â60 cm off the floor, with clean litter and a roll-away or sloped floor where possible.
  • Budget the house cost per egg (Table 2, last row) and compare it against your expected egg price before building. If house cost per egg exceeds 15 % of your egg price, reduce construction spec or increase bird numbers.
  • Keep a written maintenance schedule: check roof, curtains, feeders, drinkers, and nests monthly. Deferred repairs raise mortality and cut egg income.
  • Record daily mortality, feed intake, and egg numbers on the house wall chart. Any sudden change is your earliest warning of a housing or health problem.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the layers production module?
options: A) To manage egg collection and storage
B) To optimize feed conversion for broilers
C) To monitor and control the health of laying hens
D) To produce consistent, high-quality eggs efficiently
quiz.explanation: The layers production module focuses on producing consistent, high-quality eggs efficiently by managing all aspects of the laying flock.

quiz.q: Which factor most directly influences egg size in a laying flock?
options: A) Hen age and body weight
quiz.explanation: Egg size is primarily influenced by hen age and body weight, with older and heavier hens generally producing larger eggs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended lighting program for laying hens to maintain optimal production?
options: A) 8 hours of light and 16 hours of dark
B) 16 hours of light and 8 hours of dark
D) 12 hours of light and 12 hours of dark
quiz.explanation: A lighting program of 16 hours light and 8 hours dark is standard to stimulate and maintain optimal egg production.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most critical for eggshell formation in laying hens?
quiz.explanation: Calcium is the most critical nutrient for eggshell formation, as the shell is composed primarily of calcium carbonate.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for laying hens to maximize production and comfort?
quiz.explanation: Laying hens perform best and are most comfortable in a temperature range of 18 to 24 degrees Celsius.

quiz.q: Which management practice helps prevent egg eating in a laying flock?
options: B) Collecting eggs frequently and providing adequate nesting space
D) Lowering light intensity to zero
quiz.explanation: Frequent egg collection and adequate nesting space reduce the opportunity for hens to peck and eat eggs.

quiz.q: What does the term feed conversion ratio measure in layers production?
options: A) The number of eggs per hen per day
B) The weight of feed consumed per egg produced
C) The amount of water consumed per hen
D) The percentage of cracked eggs
quiz.explanation: Feed conversion ratio in layers production measures the weight of feed consumed per egg produced, indicating efficiency.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key indicator of flock health and productivity in layers?
options: C) Egg production rate and egg quality
quiz.explanation: Egg production rate and egg quality are key indicators of flock health and productivity in layers production.
